discovery: Discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos and the founding of neutrino astronomy with the IceCube Neutrino Observatory
motivation: Francis Halzen conceived and led IceCube, a cubic-kilometre detector built into the Antarctic ice, which in 2013 discovered a diffuse flux of astrophysical neutrinos at TeV-PeV energies, a messenger long predicted but never seen. IceCube then identified the first individual sources: the blazar TXS 0506+056 (2017-2018, through a real-time alert and multi-messenger follow-up) and the Seyfert galaxy NGC 1068 (2022), and mapped neutrino emission from the Galactic plane (2023). Christian Spiering pioneered the large-volume detection technique in natural media through Baikal and AMANDA, proving the concept that made IceCube possible and shaping the European program now continued by KM3NeT. Together, their bold detector concepts and decades of patient effort opened a new window onto the universe, giving direct access to cosmic accelerators that photons cannot reveal.
